clauses: Here is a model that passed every gate.
Fine-tuned on a store's customer conversations,
it answered seventy-two point five percent of a held-out test correctly,
up from zero before training,
and every answer was well formed.
And every one of its answers ended with a case number the customer had never given.
It was making them up.
The gate could not see it,
because it only checked that the right answer was in there somewhere.
The training data had taught it:
every reply in the transcripts ended with a number the support system had assigned.
This is the problem this platform is built around.
Not training a model,
but knowing whether to trust one,
and being able to show why.
So this is a governance platform for the whole path,
from a customer's raw data to a model a person approves.
Agents do the work at every stage:
prepare the data,
train,
evaluate,
deploy,
monitor.
Each works inside written limits:
a budget for retries,
permissions for its own stage only,
and an instruction to escalate instead of guessing.
Every stage leaves evidence behind,
in a form a reviewer can check:
which data,
which rules removed what,
which scores,
with what confidence,
at what cost.
And the last step belongs to a person.
The pipeline can register a model.
It cannot approve one.
Its own permissions deny it.
It is built as four planes.
The pipeline plane is a deterministic Step Functions spine,
thirty nine states,
that hands each stage to an agent and waits;
eight Lambdas sit around it.
The data plane is a lakehouse in S3 Tables:
raw data lands in Bronze,
where personal data stays;
Silver applies named rules,
redacting personal data,
removing duplicates,
and stripping identifiers the customer never gave;
Gold splits it for training,
and a fingerprinted extract is what the model learns from.
The governance plane turns a judged model into evidence:
gates with confidence intervals,
a provenance card on the registered model,
and SageMaker Unified Studio,
where a person reviews it.
The audit plane reconciles what every run actually cost.
No agent loop here is hand-written.
Each of the seven agents is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness:
the model,
the instructions,
the tools,
the skills and the limits are declared as configuration,
and AWS runs the loop in a session of its own,
with a shell and a file system.
That is what lets an agent run the job instead of describing it.
Nineteen skill mounts across the seven harnesses come from a pinned copy in S3,
so a skill library moving on its own cannot change what ran.
Changing behaviour is a configuration change,
reviewed like code.
And when a model provider has a bad hour,
the harnesses can switch models without a redeploy.
Four decisions carry the design.
First,
gates fail closed:
only a literal pass passes,
and a score decides on its confidence interval,
not on a lucky point estimate.
Second,
the measuring instrument is fixed.
For the checks that matter,
the agent must download a canonical scorer and run it unchanged,
so a measure cannot drift between runs.
Third,
every claim is derived from its source:
the agent count from the configs,
the state count from the state machine,
the rules on the architecture diagram from the code that runs them.
Fourth,
every guard has been watched to fail:
each one is deliberately broken in turn,
to prove it would have caught the break.
Here is what ran,
end to end,
through the pipeline.
Raw records for a store were generated,
built into Bronze,
Silver and Gold,
with thirty pieces of personal data redacted,
and a model was trained on the extract,
judged,
deployed,
tested and torn down,
for about forty-five cents of compute.
On one hundred and twenty held-out questions,
the untrained model matched zero;
the trained one matched seventy-two point five percent.
Then the gate learned to check identifiers,
and the same model failed:
zero answers out of one hundred and twenty were free of invented numbers.
With the rule added to the data,
a new model passed:
one hundred and twenty out of one hundred and twenty,
with answer quality unchanged.
A person rejected the first and approved the second.
And you can see all of it.
This console is LLMOps Governance,
the operator's view.
The pipeline tab shows every stage of a run as it happens,
including the data stages.
The outcome tab puts a trained model next to its untrained baseline on the same questions,
with the data journey,
the training numbers,
the cost and the answers side by side.
The data tab shows what each rule caught.
The cost tab prices every run.
And the same evidence is on the model's own page in Unified Studio,
where the approval happens.
That is the takeaway:
not a faster way to train a model,
but a way to know which model to trust,
and to show why.
